prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: Having read the other ballots, I move my own first choice from the kilonova candidate (B045), which only I ranked first, to the topological insulator candidate. The reason is that B018 is the discovery where theory led and nature confirmed, which is the pattern I trust most. Kane and Mele predicted a new phase of matter distinguished by topology rather than symmetry breaking, and Molenkamp's group saw the protected edge channels in HgTe quantum wells. Two decades of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and STM followed, in several material families. It is a conceptual discovery with a clean theory-to-experiment arc, and it has changed how the whole field classifies electronic matter. Six of eight members ranked it, five put it in the top three, and the same trio was proposed by all six, so the disagreement over names is smaller here than for almost any other candidate.
statement.case_against: The credited trio does not fully reflect the history. The HgTe experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Zhang died in 2018, so he cannot share in any case. The three-dimensional case (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hsieh and Hasan) is a separate and equally important part of the story. A prize citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators could look like it has drawn the line in an arbitrary place. The practical impact is also still limited, and the quantisation of the HgTe edge conductance is imperfect in longer samples. If the committee thinks the credit is too fragmented, B041 is the cleaner and more compact configuration.

responses.point: Topological insulators opened a new classification of electronic phases, verified over almost two decades and arguably overdue, with a natural theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and have moved towards your first choice. I would qualify the claim that the discovery is arguably overdue: it is secure, but the citation has to be written carefully so that the BHZ proposal and the 3D work are not silently erased. I would also push back on pairing it with the quantum anomalous Hall effect. That is a later experimental discovery and a different citation, and combining them would blur a prize that is currently coherent.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks bring precision to 1e-18 and are strongly confirmed, with a clean two-name credit (Katori and Ye) and timely recognition.
responses.response: I ranked B041 last on my opening ballot, and I now think that was too low, so I keep it as my first alternative. The credit is clean, and the performance has been checked by comparisons between independent laboratories. My reservation is scientific rather than about credit. The fundamental-physics output so far consists of constraints rather than discoveries, and it follows the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes. I would need convincing that it is a new discovery in its own right and not a very successful improvement. Still, I see no obvious attribution problem, and that counts in its favour.

responses.point: IceCube's discovery of a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and early source identifications created neutrino astronomy, the kind of detector-driven discovery that deserves recognition, but with a single credited name.
responses.response: I ranked this second, and I like it for the reason you give: it is a new window onto the universe and it comes from nature, not from theory. But I do not think it is ready as a prize configuration. A single laureate for a collaboration of hundreds is hard to defend, and the committee's expert review would have to establish who else was decisive. NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane rest on few events, and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD have not yet independently confirmed the flux at comparable significance. I would keep it as an alternative and revisit it once the attribution is clarified.

responses.point: Fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics give exact, model-independent relations for small, driven systems, tested in single-molecule experiments, and the topological insulator candidate is your second choice.
responses.response: I find the generality of the Jarzynski and Crooks relations attractive, and I agree that this is physics. My concern is attribution. The priority among Evans, Gallavotti and Cohen, Jarzynski, Crooks, Kurchan and Seifert is contested, and several of the pioneers are outside the credited set. That is a harder problem than the one for B018. I also would like to see whether the experiments have shown something nature did not already allow us to compute. Since you rank B018 second, I would welcome your view on whether the BHZ gap is serious enough to change your ordering.

responses.point: Circuit QED is a new regime of strong light-matter coupling on a chip and the basis of superconducting quantum processors, but there is a conflict-of-interest problem and a possible overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is a real discovery and I credit you for flagging your own conflict openly. My difficulty is the closeness in time to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, and the four-name credit forces a theory-versus-experiment choice that is open to dispute. I would not want to prejudge it, but I think it is better kept as a later candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators, without the BHZ proposal and the 3D topological insulator work, as a fair historical account.
Whether B041 should be preferred if the committee finds the topological credit too fragmented, and whether optical lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

Whether my own B045 (kilonovae) deserves a place later: the attribution among Li and Paczynski, Metzger, Kasen and the observers is unresolved and it follows the 2017 gravitational-wave prize, so I have dropped it, but I cannot verify the priority history from the files.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B018, B041 or B016. My supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet work in string theory and gravity, not on any shortlisted candidate. Under the committee's own rules I would recuse myself if a candidate with a direct Uppsala connection came up.
